09-01.script:
On the first of September in 1939, before dawn, German tanks and planes crossed the border into Poland. Two days later Britain and France declared war. The Second World War had begun, and it would last six terrible years.

In 1859, an English astronomer named Richard Carrington was sketching sunspots when he saw two brilliant flashes of white light on the Sun. Hours later, the greatest solar storm on record struck the Earth. Telegraph wires sparked, and the northern lights glowed as far south as the tropics.

In 1878, Emma Nutt became the world's first woman telephone operator, in Boston.

In 1914, at Cincinnati Zoo, a bird named Martha died. She was the last passenger pigeon, a species that had once flown in flocks of billions.

And in 1985, a team led by Robert Ballard sent a camera sled down into the dark of the North Atlantic, and saw the wreck of the Titanic for the first time in seventy-three years.

events.text: King Louis XIV of France dies after a 72-year reign.
Richard Carrington observes the solar flare behind the greatest geomagnetic storm on record.
Emma Nutt becomes the first woman telephone operator.
Martha, the last passenger pigeon, dies.
The Great Kantō earthquake devastates Tokyo and Yokohama.
Germany invades Poland, starting the Second World War.
The Life Insurance Corporation of India is founded.
The first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement opens in Belgrade.
Muammar Gaddafi seizes power in Libya.
Bobby Fischer becomes world chess champion.
Korean Air Lines Flight 007 is shot down by a Soviet fighter.
The wreck of the Titanic is found.

births.text: Edgar Rice Burroughs, creator of Tarzan
A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, founder of ISKCON
Barry Gibb, singer of the Bee Gees
Padma Lakshmi, author and TV host

facts.text: During the Carrington storm, some telegraph operators found they could send messages with their batteries unplugged.
Passenger pigeons were once probably the most numerous bird in North America.

09-02.script:
On the second of September in 1666, a fire started in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane in London. Fanned by a strong east wind, it raged for four days, destroying more than thirteen thousand houses and the old St Paul's Cathedral. Out of the ashes, Christopher Wren built a new city.

In 1752, people across Britain and its colonies went to bed on the second of September and woke up on the fourteenth. The country had switched calendars, and eleven days simply disappeared.

In 1945, aboard the battleship Missouri in Tokyo Bay, Japan signed its formal surrender, ending the Second World War. That same day in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh declared the independence of Vietnam.

In 1946, Jawaharlal Nehru took office at the head of India's interim government, a step on the road to freedom.

And in 1969, a bank in New York installed one of America's first cash machines. Its advertisement read: "On Sept. 2, our bank will open at 9:00 and never close again."

events.text: The Great Fire of London begins.
Britain's last day on the Julian calendar.
The US Treasury Department is founded.
Auroras from the Carrington storm are seen as far south as the Caribbean.
Theodore Roosevelt first uses the phrase 'Speak softly and carry a big stick'.
Japan formally surrenders aboard USS Missouri.
Ho Chi Minh declares the independence of Vietnam.
India's interim government, led by Nehru, takes office.
The CBS Evening News becomes network TV's first half-hour nightly news.
One of the first American ATMs opens in New York.

births.text: Christa McAuliffe, American teacher and astronaut

facts.text: The Great Fire of London's officially recorded death toll was only six people, though the real number is unknown.
The Monument in London is 61 metres tall, the same as its distance from where the Great Fire started.

09-03.script:
On the third of September in 1939, at a quarter past eleven in the morning, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain spoke to Britain on the radio. Germany had not answered the British ultimatum, he said, and "consequently this country is at war with Germany." France followed that afternoon.

In 1783, in Paris, Britain signed a treaty recognising the independence of the United States of America.

In 1838, a young man named Frederick Douglass disguised himself as a sailor and escaped from slavery in Maryland. He became one of the greatest voices for freedom in American history.

In 1967, at five o'clock in the morning, every car in Sweden stopped, carefully crossed to the other side of the road, and set off again. Sweden had switched to driving on the right.

In 1976, the Viking Two lander touched down on Mars.

And in 1995, a programmer in California started a website to auction things online. It became eBay.

events.text: Richard the Lionheart is crowned King of England.
Oliver Cromwell dies.
The Treaty of Paris ends the American Revolutionary War.
Frederick Douglass escapes from slavery.
Malcolm Campbell becomes the first to drive a car faster than 300 miles an hour.
Britain and France declare war on Germany.
Sweden switches to driving on the right.
Qatar becomes independent.

births.text: Carl David Anderson, discoverer of the positron

Sweden's switch to the right was called Dagen H, 'H Day', for 'Högertrafik', right-hand traffic.

09-04.script:
On the fourth of September in 1882, at three o'clock in the afternoon, Thomas Edison threw a switch at his Pearl Street power station in Manhattan. In the offices of the New York Times and the banks of Wall Street, electric light bulbs flickered on. It was the first central power station in America, and the beginning of the electric age.

In 476, the last Roman emperor in the west, a boy named Romulus Augustulus, was removed from his throne.

In 1781, a group of forty-four settlers founded a small town in California. It became Los Angeles.

In 1886, the Apache leader Geronimo surrendered to the United States army in Arizona.

In 1888, George Eastman patented a simple camera loaded with a roll of film, and registered a new name, Kodak. "You press the button," he promised, "we do the rest."

And in 1998, two Stanford students, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, founded a company to organise the world's information. It was called Google.

Los Angeles is founded.
The French Third Republic is proclaimed.
Edison's Pearl Street power station begins supplying electricity.
Geronimo surrenders.
George Eastman patents his roll-film camera and registers the name Kodak.

The Little Rock Nine are blocked from entering their high school.
Google is founded.
Naturalist Steve Irwin dies.

births.text: Dadabhai Naoroji, the 'Grand Old Man of India'

facts.text: Eastman chose the name Kodak because K was his favourite letter and the word was short and hard to misspell.
Google's name comes from 'googol', the number 1 followed by 100 zeros.
Dadabhai Naoroji was the first Indian elected to the British Parliament.

09-05.script:
On the fifth of September in 1888, Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan was born in a small town in Tamil Nadu. He became a great philosopher and India's second President. When his students asked to celebrate his birthday, he asked them instead to honour all teachers. Since then, India has celebrated today as Teachers' Day.

In 1774, delegates from twelve American colonies met in Philadelphia for the First Continental Congress.

In 1882, ten thousand workers marched through New York in America's first Labor Day parade.

In 1960, at the Rome Olympics, an eighteen-year-old boxer named Cassius Clay won gold. The world would come to know him as Muhammad Ali.

In 1977, Voyager One was launched. It is now the most distant human-made object, more than twenty-four billion kilometres from home.

And in 1997, Mother Teresa died in Calcutta. The International Day of Charity is held on the anniversary of her death.

events.text: The First Continental Congress meets.
The first Labor Day parade is held in New York.
The first gasoline pump is delivered, to a shop in Fort Wayne, Indiana.
The Treaty of Portsmouth ends the Russo-Japanese War.
The First Battle of the Marne begins.
Cassius Clay wins Olympic boxing gold.
Terrorists take Israeli athletes hostage at the Munich Olympics.

facts.text: Voyager 1 carries a golden record with sounds and greetings from Earth in 55 languages.
Freddie Mercury was born Farrokh Bulsara in Zanzibar.

09-06.script:
On the sixth of September in 1522, a battered ship named Victoria limped into the Spanish port of Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Three years earlier, five ships and about two hundred and seventy men had set out with Magellan. Now just eighteen sick and starving sailors came home. But they had done something no one had ever done before: they had sailed all the way around the world.

In 1620, the Mayflower set sail from Plymouth in England with a hundred and two passengers bound for America.

In 1901, President William McKinley was shot while shaking hands with the public in Buffalo, New York. He died eight days later.

In 1968, Swaziland, now Eswatini, became independent.

In 1991, the city of Leningrad took back its old name, Saint Petersburg.

And in 2018, India's Supreme Court struck down an old colonial law against gay relationships. "History owes an apology," one of the judges wrote.

The Mayflower sets sail from Plymouth.
President McKinley is shot in Buffalo.
Robert Peary announces by telegraph that he has reached the North Pole.

births.text: Jane Addams, Nobel Peace Prize winner

facts.text: John Dalton was colour-blind, and colour blindness was once called 'Daltonism'.
Of Magellan's five ships, only the Victoria made it back to Spain.

09-07.script:
On the seventh of September in 1822, beside the Ipiranga stream near São Paulo, the Portuguese prince Pedro received letters from Lisbon ordering him home. He drew his sword and cried, "Independence or death!" Brazil became an independent empire, with Pedro as its emperor.

In 1927, in a San Francisco laboratory, a twenty-one-year-old inventor named Philo Farnsworth sent a simple straight line from a camera to a screen. It was the first image transmitted by fully electronic television.

In 1936, in a zoo in Hobart, the last known thylacine, the Tasmanian tiger, died of cold one night. Australia now marks today as Threatened Species Day.

In 1940, German bombers began the Blitz on London. For fifty-seven nights in a row, the city was bombed.

And in 2019, in the early hours of the morning in India, the Vikram lander of Chandrayaan Two fell silent just before landing on the Moon. Four years later, its successor would succeed.

The James–Younger Gang's raid on Northfield, Minnesota, fails.

facts.text: Farnsworth said the idea for scanning a TV picture line by line came to him while ploughing a field as a teenager.
Despite its stripes, the thylacine was a marsupial, more closely related to kangaroos than to tigers.

09-08.script:
On the eighth of September in 1504, Michelangelo's statue of David was unveiled in the main square of Florence. Carved from a block of marble that other sculptors had given up on, the young giant-slayer stood more than five metres tall. The people of Florence saw in him their own city: small, brave and free.

In 1900, a hurricane struck the island city of Galveston in Texas with no proper warning. It remains the deadliest natural disaster in American history.

In 1941, German forces closed the ring around Leningrad. The siege would last almost nine hundred days.

In 1944, the first V-2 rocket fell on London, arriving faster than sound, without warning.

In 1966, a new television series about a starship and its crew first went on air. It was called Star Trek.

And in 2022, Queen Elizabeth the Second died at Balmoral, after seventy years on the throne.

Today is International Literacy Day.

St. Augustine, Florida, the oldest continuously inhabited European settlement in the US, is founded.

Michelangelo's David was carved from a block of marble that had lain unused for about 25 years.

09-09.script:
On the ninth of September in 1947, the team working on the Harvard Mark Two computer found it was making mistakes. Searching inside, they found a moth trapped in one of its relays. They taped the insect into their logbook with a note: "First actual case of bug being found." Computer bugs had been named.

In 1776, the Continental Congress decided that the new nation would be called the United States of America.

In 1850, California became the thirty-first American state.

In 1892, the astronomer Edward Barnard discovered Amalthea, a small moon of Jupiter, the last moon ever found by eye through a telescope.

In 1956, Elvis Presley appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show, and around sixty million people watched.

And in 1976, Mao Zedong, who had ruled China since 1949, died in Beijing.

In the Himalayan state of Uttarakhand, today is Himalaya Diwas, a day to protect the mountains.

09-10.script:
On the tenth of September in 2008, at CERN on the border of France and Switzerland, scientists watched their screens as the first beam of protons travelled all the way around the Large Hadron Collider, a ring twenty-seven kilometres long buried deep underground. Four years later, it would find the Higgs boson.

In 1846, Elias Howe received a patent for a sewing machine that used two threads to make a lockstitch, the stitch that most machines still use.

In 1897, a London taxi driver named George Smith crashed into a building and became the first person ever arrested for driving while drunk.

In 1898, Empress Elisabeth of Austria, known as Sisi, was stabbed by an anarchist on the shore of Lake Geneva.

In 1977, in Marseille, France carried out its last execution by guillotine.

And in 2002, Switzerland, long proud of its neutrality, joined the United Nations.

Today is World Suicide Prevention Day, a reminder that no one should struggle alone.

09-11.script:
On the eleventh of September in 1893, at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago, a young monk from India in an orange robe stood up to speak. He began with five words: "Sisters and brothers of America." The audience of thousands rose and applauded for two minutes. Swami Vivekananda went on to speak of tolerance and of all faiths as paths to the same truth.

Thirteen years later to the day, in 1906, at a meeting in Johannesburg, Mohandas Gandhi led Indians in a vow to resist an unjust law peacefully. The idea he called satyagraha was born.

In 1297, William Wallace defeated an English army at Stirling Bridge.

In 1609, Henry Hudson sailed into the bay at the mouth of the river that now bears his name, beside the island of Manhattan.

And in 2001, terrorists flew hijacked planes into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. Nearly three thousand people died, and the world changed.

Swami Vivekananda addresses the Parliament of the World's Religions.

facts.text: Vivekananda's Chicago speech is remembered every year in India on 11 September.
The Pentagon's construction began exactly 60 years before the 2001 attack on it.
Vinoba Bhave walked across India asking landowners to give land to the landless.

09-12.script:
On the twelfth of September in 1897, on a rocky ridge in the North-West Frontier, twenty-one Sikh soldiers of the 36th Sikhs held the small signalling post of Saragarhi against an attack by thousands of tribesmen. They refused to surrender and fought to the last man. Every one of them was awarded the Indian Order of Merit, and the Sikh Regiment remembers them today.

In 1940, four teenagers in the south of France followed their dog down a hole near Lascaux and found a cave whose walls were covered with paintings of horses, bulls and deer, painted some seventeen thousand years ago.

In 1959, the Soviet Union launched Luna Two, which became the first human-made object to reach the Moon.

In 1962, at Rice University in Texas, President Kennedy declared, "We choose to go to the Moon in this decade, not because it is easy, but because it is hard."

And in 1992, Mae Jemison flew aboard the space shuttle Endeavour, the first African American woman in space.

Switzerland adopts its federal constitution.
Twenty-one Sikh soldiers make their last stand at Saragarhi.

The Lascaux cave was closed to visitors in 1963 because people's breath was damaging the paintings.

09-13.script:
On the thirteenth of September in 1814, British warships began bombarding Fort McHenry, which guarded the harbour of Baltimore. All through the night, a young lawyer named Francis Scott Key watched the rockets and bombs from a ship in the harbour. At dawn he saw the American flag still flying, and wrote a poem that became the Star-Spangled Banner.

In 1759, on the Plains of Abraham outside Quebec City, the British defeated the French in a battle of barely an hour, deciding the future of Canada.

In 1899, a man named Henry Bliss stepped off a streetcar in New York and was struck by a taxi. He was the first person killed by a car in America.

In 1948, the Indian Army entered the state of Hyderabad, and within five days it had joined India.

In 1959, Luna Two crashed into the Moon, the first spacecraft to reach another world.

And in 1985, a plumber named Mario first jumped onto television screens in Japan, in Super Mario Bros.

Today is Roald Dahl Day.

Britain defeats France on the Plains of Abraham.
The bombardment of Fort McHenry inspires 'The Star-Spangled Banner'.

facts.text: Roald Dahl was a fighter pilot in the Second World War before he became a writer.
Luna 2 carried metal pennants with the Soviet coat of arms, which scattered across the Moon.

09-14.script:
On the fourteenth of September in 1949, the Constituent Assembly of India agreed that Hindi, written in the Devanagari script, would be the official language of the Union. The date was also the birthday of the writer Beohar Rajendra Simha, who had worked hard for it. India celebrates today as Hindi Diwas.

In 1752, Britain woke up on the fourteenth of September, the day after the second. The Gregorian calendar had arrived.

In 1812, Napoleon's Grand Army entered Moscow, only to find the city abandoned. That night, fires began to burn.

In 1814, Francis Scott Key, having watched the bombardment of Fort McHenry, wrote the words of the Star-Spangled Banner.

In 1901, Theodore Roosevelt became President after McKinley died.

And in 2015, two detectors in Louisiana and Washington State trembled by less than the width of a proton. They had felt gravitational waves from two black holes that collided more than a billion years ago, just as Einstein had predicted.

Napoleon's army enters Moscow.

births.text: Robert Cecil, Nobel Peace Prize winner

facts.text: Zond 5's tortoises became the first living things to travel around the Moon and return.
Hindi is spoken by more than 600 million people, counting second-language speakers.

09-15.script:
On the fifteenth of September in 1861, Mokshagundam Visvesvaraya was born in a village in Karnataka. He became one of India's greatest engineers, building dams and irrigation systems and designing flood defences for Hyderabad. India celebrates his birthday as Engineer's Day.

In 1830, the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened, the first line to carry passengers between two cities entirely by steam locomotives. On the opening day, a politician named William Huskisson stepped onto the track and was struck by Stephenson's Rocket.

In 1835, HMS Beagle reached the Galápagos Islands, and a young naturalist named Charles Darwin began studying their strange finches and giant tortoises.

In 1916, at the Somme, British tanks went into battle for the first time.

In 1959, Doordarshan began broadcasting from Delhi, the start of television in India.

And in 2017, the Cassini spacecraft, low on fuel after thirteen years at Saturn, plunged into the planet's clouds, sending data until the very end.

Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote Devdas, filmed many times in India.

names: International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer
09-16.script:
On the sixteenth of September in 1987, in Montreal, the nations of the world agreed to phase out the chemicals that were eating a hole in the ozone layer, the thin shield of gas that protects the Earth from the Sun's harshest rays. The Montreal Protocol worked, and the ozone layer is slowly healing. Today is World Ozone Day.

In 1810, in the small town of Dolores, the priest Miguel Hidalgo rang his church bell and called on the people to rise against Spanish rule. Mexico celebrates the Cry of Dolores as its independence day.

In 1916, the singer M. S. Subbulakshmi was born in Madurai. She would become the first musician awarded the Bharat Ratna.

In 1959, the Xerox 914, the first easy-to-use plain-paper copier, was demonstrated in New York.

And in 1963, Malaya, Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak came together to form Malaysia, which celebrates today as Malaysia Day.

The Montreal Protocol is the first UN treaty to be ratified by every country in the world.

09-17.script:
On the seventeenth of September in 1787, in a hot assembly room in Philadelphia, thirty-nine delegates signed the Constitution of the United States. "We the People," it began. Benjamin Franklin, then eighty-one, said he had often wondered whether the sun carved on George Washington's chair was rising or setting. Now, he said, he knew it was rising.

In 1862, at Antietam Creek in Maryland, more Americans were killed or wounded than on any other single day in the nation's history.

In 1908, Lieutenant Thomas Selfridge flew as a passenger with Orville Wright. The plane crashed, and Selfridge became the first person to die in a powered aeroplane.

In 1948, the Nizam of Hyderabad surrendered to the Indian Army, and his state became part of India.

In 1978, at Camp David, Egypt and Israel agreed a framework for peace.

And in 1991, Linus Torvalds released the first version of Linux, the free software that now runs most of the world's servers and every Android phone.

09-18.script:
On the eighteenth of September in 1977, the Voyager One spacecraft, already eleven million kilometres from home, turned its camera back towards the Earth. It took the first picture ever to show the whole Earth and Moon together in a single frame: two thin crescents floating in the dark.

In 1793, George Washington laid the cornerstone of the Capitol building in Washington.

In 1810, the people of Santiago formed their own government, the first step towards Chile's independence, and Chileans celebrate today with dancing and empanadas.

In 1851, the first edition of the New York Daily Times, now the New York Times, went on sale for one cent.

In 1879, the people of Blackpool gathered on the seafront to see eight electric arc lamps light up the promenade, the beginning of the famous Blackpool Illuminations.

In 1931, an explosion on a railway line near Mukden gave Japan an excuse to invade Manchuria.

And in 1970, the guitarist Jimi Hendrix died in London, aged just twenty-seven.

Samuel Johnson's Dictionary of the English Language took him about nine years to write.

names: International Talk Like a Pirate Day
09-19.script:
On the nineteenth of September in 1893, New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world to give women the right to vote in national elections. Kate Sheppard and her fellow campaigners had gathered petitions signed by nearly a third of the country's adult women. Their portraits are now on New Zealand's ten-dollar note.

In 1783, at the Palace of Versailles, the Montgolfier brothers sent a sheep, a duck and a rooster up in a hot-air balloon, while King Louis the Sixteenth watched. All three landed safely.

In 1960, India and Pakistan signed the Indus Waters Treaty, sharing the rivers of the Indus basin.

In 1982, a computer scientist named Scott Fahlman suggested marking jokes on an online message board with a colon, a dash and a bracket. The smiley had been born.

And in 1991, two hikers in the Alps found a body in melting ice. He was Ötzi, a man who had died more than five thousand years ago.

Today is International Talk Like a Pirate Day. Arr!

events.text: England defeats France at the Battle of Poitiers.

09-20.script:
On the twentieth of September in 1857, after a siege of more than three months, British troops fought their way back into Delhi, street by street. The last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, fled to Humayun's Tomb and was captured soon afterwards. The great uprising of 1857 was being crushed, and the Mughal Empire was at an end.

In 1519, Ferdinand Magellan's fleet left the Spanish coast at Sanlúcar for the open Atlantic.

In 1870, Italian troops broke through the walls of Rome near the Porta Pia, and Rome became the capital of a united Italy.

In 1946, the first Cannes Film Festival opened on the French Riviera.

In 1967, the great liner Queen Elizabeth Two was launched on the River Clyde.

And in 1973, in front of thirty thousand people in Houston and millions on television, Billie Jean King beat Bobby Riggs in a tennis match called the Battle of the Sexes.

The QE2 sailed more than 9 million kilometres in her career.

09-21.script:
On the twenty-first of September in 1937, a London publisher brought out a children's book by an Oxford professor of Old English. It began: "In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit." The first printing of The Hobbit sold out by Christmas, and J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-earth had begun to grow.

In 1792, the new National Convention in Paris abolished the French monarchy.

In 1897, the New York Sun answered a letter from an eight-year-old girl who asked if Santa Claus was real. "Yes, Virginia," the editor wrote, "there is a Santa Claus."

In 1964, Malta became independent, followed on this same date by Belize in 1981 and Armenia in 1991.

And in 2003, after eight years exploring Jupiter and its moons, the Galileo spacecraft was steered into the giant planet to burn up, so it could never contaminate the icy moon Europa, which might hold life.

Today is the International Day of Peace.

The UN's Peace Bell in New York was cast from coins donated by people from about 60 nations.

09-22.script:
On the twenty-second of September in 1791, in a poor family in south London, Michael Faraday was born. He left school at thirteen to work for a bookbinder, and read the science books he bound. He went on to discover how to make electricity from magnetism, and every power station on Earth works because of him.

In 1499, the Treaty of Basel made the Swiss cantons effectively independent of the Holy Roman Empire.

In 1539, Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism, passed away at Kartarpur.

In 1862, President Lincoln announced that slaves in the rebelling states would be freed on the first day of the new year.

In 1888, the first issue of National Geographic magazine was published.

In 1980, Iraq invaded Iran, beginning a war that lasted eight years.

And in 1994, six friends in a New York coffee shop first appeared on television. The show was called Friends.

Today is World Rhino Day, and World Rose Day, for people living with cancer.

facts.text: There are five species of rhinoceros, three of them in Asia.
Faraday turned down a knighthood and the presidency of the Royal Society.

09-23.script:
On the twenty-third of September in 1846, at the Berlin Observatory, the astronomer Johann Galle received a letter from the French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier. Le Verrier had calculated where an unseen planet must be, from the way it tugged on Uranus. That very night Galle pointed his telescope at the spot and found it within an hour. Neptune was the first planet found by mathematics.

In 1803, at Assaye in the Deccan, a young British general named Arthur Wellesley, the future Duke of Wellington, defeated the Maratha army in a fierce battle he later called his finest.

In 1806, the explorers Lewis and Clark returned to St Louis after more than two years crossing America to the Pacific and back.

In 1889, a small company in Kyoto began making playing cards. It was called Nintendo.

In 1913, the French aviator Roland Garros made the first flight across the Mediterranean Sea.

And in 1932, the lands of Ibn Saud were united as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

Galileo saw Neptune in 1612 and 1613 but thought it was a star.

09-24.script:
On the twenty-fourth of September in 2014, just after eight in the morning, scientists at ISRO in Bengaluru waited for a signal from two hundred million kilometres away. It came: Mangalyaan was in orbit around Mars. India became the first country to reach Mars on its first attempt, and the mission cost less than some Hollywood films about space.

In 1852, the French engineer Henri Giffard flew a steam-powered airship from Paris, the first powered and steerable flight.

In 1869, two speculators tried to corner the American gold market, and on Black Friday the price collapsed and fortunes were lost.

In 1932, in Yerwada jail near Pune, Gandhi and B. R. Ambedkar reached the Poona Pact on the representation of the depressed classes, ending Gandhi's fast.

In 1948, Soichiro Honda founded a company to make motorcycles.

And in 1960, the USS Enterprise, the first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, was launched in Virginia.

09-25.script:
On the twenty-fifth of September in 1513, the Spanish explorer Vasco Núñez de Balboa climbed a peak in the jungles of Panama and saw, stretching away to the south, a vast ocean. He was the first European to see the Pacific from the Americas. Days later he waded into the water in full armour and claimed it all for Spain.

In 1066, at Stamford Bridge in Yorkshire, King Harold of England defeated a Norwegian invasion. Three days later, the Normans landed in the south.

In 1789, the American Congress approved the amendments that became the Bill of Rights.

In 1956, the first telephone cable under the Atlantic began carrying calls between Britain and North America.

In 1957, soldiers escorted nine Black students into Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas.

And in 1981, Sandra Day O'Connor was sworn in as the first woman on the United States Supreme Court.

It is also the birthday, in 1916, of the thinker Deendayal Upadhyaya.

facts.text: Balboa named it the 'South Sea'; Magellan later called it the Pacific, meaning peaceful.

names: International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons
09-26.script:
On the twenty-sixth of September in 1983, a Soviet officer named Stanislav Petrov was on duty at a secret bunker near Moscow when the alarms began to wail. The computers said five American missiles were flying towards the Soviet Union. Petrov had minutes to decide whether to report an attack. He judged it a false alarm, and he was right. Some say he saved the world.

In 1580, Francis Drake sailed the Golden Hind into Plymouth, the first English captain to sail around the world.

In 1820, the great Bengali reformer Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar was born. He fought for the education of girls and for widows' right to remarry.

In 1960, John Kennedy and Richard Nixon faced each other in the first televised presidential debate.

In 1969, the Beatles released Abbey Road, with its famous cover of the four crossing a zebra crossing.

And in 1932, Manmohan Singh was born in a village in Punjab. He would become Prime Minister of India.

09-27.script:
On the twenty-seventh of September in 1825, in the north of England, a crowd watched George Stephenson's engine Locomotion pull a train of wagons along the new Stockton and Darlington Railway. It carried coal, flour and hundreds of passengers. It was the first public railway to use steam engines.

In 1822, the French scholar Jean-François Champollion announced that he had cracked the code of Egyptian hieroglyphs, using the Rosetta Stone.

In 1833, the reformer Raja Ram Mohan Roy, who campaigned against sati and for modern education, died in Bristol, England.

In 1905, a young patent clerk in Bern named Albert Einstein sent a short paper to a physics journal. It contained the idea that would become E equals m c squared.

In 1908, the first Ford Model T rolled out of a factory in Detroit.

And in 1962, Rachel Carson published Silent Spring, a book about pesticides that helped start the modern environmental movement.

names: International Day for Universal Access to Information
09-28.script:
On the twenty-eighth of September in 1907, in a village in Punjab, a boy named Bhagat Singh was born. He grew into a fearless revolutionary who read deeply, wrote fiercely and went to the gallows at twenty-three, shouting "Inquilab Zindabad!" Long live the revolution.

In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming came back from holiday to his messy laboratory in London and noticed that a mould had killed the bacteria on one of his dishes. He had discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic.

In 1895, Louis Pasteur, who created the first rabies vaccine, died near Paris. Today is World Rabies Day.

In 1924, two American planes landed in Seattle, completing the first flight around the world. It had taken almost six months.

And in 1929, Lata Mangeshkar was born in Indore. Over more than seventy years, the Nightingale of India sang thousands of songs.

In 2008, SpaceX's Falcon One became the first privately built liquid-fuelled rocket to reach orbit.

facts.text: Fleming later said: 'One sometimes finds what one is not looking for.'

09-29.script:
On the twenty-ninth of September in 1829, the first officers of the new Metropolitan Police began walking the streets of London in blue tailcoats and top hats. They were nicknamed Bobbies and Peelers, after Sir Robert Peel, who had founded the force. They carried no guns, and most British police still do not.

In 1885, the first electric tram in Britain began running along the seafront at Blackpool.

In 1938, at a conference in Munich, the leaders of Britain, France and Italy agreed to let Hitler take a large part of Czechoslovakia. Chamberlain came home promising "peace for our time." It lasted less than a year.

In 1954, twelve European countries founded CERN, a laboratory near Geneva to study the smallest pieces of matter.

And in 1988, the space shuttle Discovery lifted off, the first shuttle launch since the Challenger disaster nearly three years earlier.

Today is World Heart Day, a good day to go for a walk.

09-30.script:
On the thirtieth of September in 1846, a dentist in Boston named William Morton held a cloth soaked in ether over a patient's face, and pulled out a tooth. The patient felt nothing at all. Within weeks, Morton had shown the world that surgery could be done without pain.

In 1791, in Vienna, Mozart's opera The Magic Flute had its first performance. Mozart died just over two months later.

In 1882, on the Fox River in Wisconsin, the world's first hydroelectric power station began to turn.

In 1938, Neville Chamberlain landed in London waving a piece of paper signed by Hitler.

In 1966, Botswana became independent.

And in 1993, before dawn, a powerful earthquake struck the district of Latur in Maharashtra, destroying villages as people slept.

Today is International Translation Day, on the feast of Saint Jerome, who translated the Bible into Latin.
